# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zero-order interpolation, Zeroth-order interpolation, box filter

## Overview
Interpolation schemes for volume rendering approximate a continuous scalar field $V(\mathbf{p})$ from discrete voxel samples $V_i$ to determine values at arbitrary query positions $\mathbf{p}$ along viewing rays [G]. This family solves the problem of discretization artifacts (such as aliasing, blockiness, or staircasing) inherent in [nearest-neighbor sampling](#1151-nearest-neighbor-density-lookup.md) by applying spatial or frequency-domain filters [S4, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Lanczos Resampling](11246-lanczos-resampling.md) and [Interpolation Functions for Resampling](15932-interpolation-functions-for-resampling.md) by encompassing the full spectrum from zero-order box filters to high-order frequency-domain sinc resampling, including specialized hardware approximations and fast GPU-accelerated cubic evaluations [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function $V(\mathbf{p})$ must be approximated from a discrete set of samples $V_i$ located at grid positions $\mathbf{p}_i$ [G]. The core mechanism involves:

1.  **Query Positioning**: Determining the 3D coordinate $\mathbf{p}$ along the ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ where a value is needed [G]. This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings [G].
2.  **Kernel/Weight Application**: Computing weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$ based on the distance between $\mathbf{p}$ and the sample centers $\mathbf{p}_i$ [G]. The interpolated value is:
    $$
    V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i
    $$
    The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S3, unofficial].
3.  **Coordinate Transformation**: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized $[-1, 1]$ or $[0, 1]$ ranges) before interpolation [G].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
[Frequency Domain Volume Rendering](#952-frequency-domain-volume-rendering.md) ([FD method](#826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)) is a [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that performs resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using [Fourier transforms](#2288-fourier-transform.md) to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing principles such as the shifting, packing, and derivative theorems to achieve the best theoretical reconstruction quality using the ideal [sinc filter](#2085-ideal-low-pass-filter-rect-filter.md). Unlike standard spatial domain methods (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or hybrid approaches that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples volume slices in object space via zero-padding, ensuring superior accuracy for high-magnification views.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
[Fast tri-cubic interpolation](#848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) is a GPU-based higher-order [interpolation method](#10526-interpolation-methods.md) that reconstructs a continuous signal from discrete volume samples using a tri-cubic B-spline filter. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with evaluating the 64-term convolution sum required for standard [tri-cubic interpolation](#1077-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) by reducing the number of texture fetches to eight. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) and [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md), by providing higher-order continuity and reduced aliasing, while distinguishing itself from [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) by operating directly in the spatial domain using separable tensor-product B-splines.

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
[Bilinear interpolation](#858-bilinear-interpolation.md) estimates the value of a function at an arbitrary point within a two-dimensional rectangular grid by using the known values at the four surrounding corner points. It extends [linear interpolation](#14935-linear-interpolation.md) from one dimension to two by applying the process sequentially along each axis, resulting in a surface that is linear along any line parallel to the coordinate axes. In the context of volume rendering, it is primarily used for sampling 2D texture maps (e.g., for textured primitives or [frequency domain rendering](#6050-fourier-volume-rendering.md)) or for interpolating values on the faces of 3D grid cells. It sets itself apart from [nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) by providing C⁰ continuity (smooth value transitions) while remaining computationally cheaper than higher-order methods like bicubic or trilinear interpolation.

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
[Hardware Interpolation Approximation](#1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md) is a volume rendering technique that leverages graphics hardware [rasterization](#15310-rasterization.md) to approximate the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md). It solves the problem of efficient ray casting by mapping the integration process to polygon subdivision and hardware-driven linear interpolation. It is distinct from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) and [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md) because the interpolation kernel is not fixed to the volume grid but is instead determined by the geometric subdivision of the view plane polygons by the graphics pipeline.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but requires approximately 5 times more computation time.

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that estimates the value of a continuous scalar field at a query point by computing a weighted average of nearby sample values, where the influence of each sample decreases as its distance from the query point increases. It is chosen when a smooth, non-linear reconstruction is required from sparse or irregular data points (such as drill-hole assays) and when the computational cost of higher-order schemes like tri-linear or tri-cubic interpolation is prohibitive or when the underlying data structure is not a [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md). Unlike [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md), which assumes a regular grid and guarantees $C^0$ continuity along interior faces, IDW is grid-agnostic and does not guarantee continuity across cell boundaries unless extended to neighboring cells.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
Variable Gaussian Blurring is a reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S6, unofficial]. It involves applying variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S6, unofficial]. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S6, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S7, unofficial]. The formula is $c = c_1 \cdot (A_2 / A) + c_2 \cdot (A_3 / A) + c_3 \cdot (A_1 / A)$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S7, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
[Adaptive Interpolation](#861-adaptive-filter-size-for-rendering-time-reduction.md) for Isosurface Detection interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate [S3, unofficial]. It uses non-binary classifiers to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S3, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used for the isovalue surface; when data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S3, unofficial]. This method supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality) [S3, unofficial].

### Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling
Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling are filters applied to extracted projection-slices to control ghosting artifacts and rendering quality during Fourier volume rendering [S8]. Point-sampling (nearest-neighbour) filter clamps missing samples to the nearest available value, causing apparent ghosting artifacts when the volume is rotated [S8]. Trilinear interpolation filter reduces replica intensities and ghosting artifacts compared to point-sampling, with similar performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$ but higher cost for larger volumes [S8]. Hamming [windowed-sinc interpolation](#18705-windowed-sinc-interpolation.md) filter with width 5 is a high-order reconstruction filter that maximally reduces ghosting artifacts when combined with zero-padding [S8]. Point-sampling and trilinear interpolation have nearly identical performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$, but trilinear incurs higher performance overhead for larger volumes [S8].

## Background
The study of interpolation schemes for volume rendering originated with the need to reconstruct continuous scalar fields from discrete voxel data for visualization [G]. Early work by Westover (1990) established the importance of [footprint evaluation](#1180-footprint-evaluation.md) and reconstruction filters in eliminating artifacts such as aliasing and blockiness [S4, S5, unofficial]. The distinction between zero-order (nearest-neighbor), first-order (linear/trilinear), and higher-order (cubic, sinc) interpolation was formalized in foundational texts and papers, highlighting the trade-off between computational cost and visual quality [S1, S3, unofficial]. The introduction of [frequency-domain methods](#9801-frequency-domain-methods.md) and later GPU implementations by Viola et al. (2004) expanded the family to include Fourier-based resampling, which offers superior quality for zooming operations [S1, S5, unofficial]. Modern implementations leverage hardware [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md), such as fast tri-cubic interpolation via texture units, to make high-order filtering practical for real-time rendering [S1, S5, unofficial].
